name: Rhode Island
$methodComment: 2026 Rhode Island Withholding Tax Booklet (RI Division of Taxation, fetched and read directly): the simplest bracket state in this project by one real measure -- 'TABLES ARE FOR ALL FILING STATUS TYPES,' i.e. ONE shared 3-tier bracket schedule (3.75/4.75/5.99%) regardless of filing status, unlike every other bracket state built this session (CA/MD/UT all branch by status). Subtract (exemptions x per-period exemption amount), look up the SAME table for everyone, done -- except for a genuine wrinkle: the exemption amount is NOT a flat per-exemption figure at every income level -- once PERIOD wages exceed a threshold (annualized: $290,800), the exemption amount becomes $0 entirely (a cliff, not Wisconsin's gradual phase-out). Genuine PER-PERIOD tables (all 8 frequencies) transcribed verbatim, not derived from the annual table, since the source's OWN worked example ($87.57) only reproduces exactly via the direct weekly table -- an annualize-then-divide reconstruction lands one cent off ($87.56), the same two-valid-methods divergence already documented for California/Missouri in this project.

sources.title: 2026 Rhode Island Employer's Income Tax Withholding Tables (RI Division of Taxation)
sources.verifiedBy: PDF downloaded and text-extracted directly, extracted CLEANLY under -layout. Reproduced the booklet's own worked example by hand (weekly $2,195, single, 1 exemption: $2,195 - $19.23 = $2,175.77 taxable; bracket [1,578-3,586, base $59.18, 4.75%]: $59.18 + 4.75%x$597.77 = $87.574 -> $87.57) BEFORE trusting the table, using the DIRECT weekly table (not an annual-derived one, which would have landed at $87.56 -- a real one-cent divergence caught by checking both paths against the source's own stated answer).

sources.title: RI Department of Labor & Training: 2026 TDI/TCI and UI Tax Rates
sources.verifiedBy: cross_source_confirmed across Bloomberg Tax and DLT's own press-release title, both agreeing: TDI rate 1.1% for 2026 (down from 1.3% in 2025), TDI/TCI taxable wage base $100,000 (up from $89,200), UI new-employer rate 1.21%, UI experience-rated range 0.9%-9.4% (Schedule F).

sources.title: Reciprocity check (Rhode Island has NONE with Massachusetts or Connecticut, its only bordering states)
sources.verifiedBy: cross_source_confirmed via multiple independent secondary sources agreeing RI-MA and RI-CT commuters both pay tax to the work state and claim an Other-State-Tax-Credit on their resident return -- no withholding-time exemption exists in either direction.

sources.title: 2026 Rhode Island Employer's Income Tax Withholding Tables -- Sections 4 and 12 (supplemental wages)
sources.verifiedBy: Same booklet already on file for this state, re-fetched and read in full for the 'find and fix anything missing across all 50 states' pass. Two sections address supplemental wages and read slightly inconsistently with each other, disclosed rather than silently reconciled: Section 4 describes ONLY the aggregate method ("if the supplemental wages are paid separately, the employer may add the supplemental wages to the regular wages paid... for the last preceding payroll period, determine the amount to be withheld as if the aggregate amount were a single payment, subtract the tax withheld for the last preceding payroll period") -- no flat rate appears there at all. Section 12 ("SUPPLEMENTAL WAGES") then states declaratively: "How you withhold on supplemental payments depends on whether the supplemental payment is identified as a separate payment from regular wages (see part 4 for details). The Supplemental withholding rate is 5.99%." That 5.99% is ALSO exactly this file's own top marginal bracket rate (bracketPerPeriodSingleTable.brackets, every period's highest tier) -- genuinely ambiguous whether Section 12 names an independent flat-rate METHOD or is simply restating what aggregation converges to for a high earner. Modelled as BOTH options being available (matching Missouri's own dual-method shape in this project) rather than picking one, since the guide's own Section 12 sentence is declarative, not descriptive prose -- but this ambiguity is recorded here rather than resolved with more confidence than the source itself supports.

bracketPerPeriodSingleTable.exemptionAmountComment: $1,000/year per exemption, cleanly divisible into every one of the engine's 8 native pay periods (weekly 1000/52=19.23, biweekly 1000/26=38.46, etc. -- no NJ/MD-style daily-divisor mismatch here).
bracketPerPeriodSingleTable.exemptionPhaseOutComment: A CLIFF, not a gradual phase-out (unlike Wisconsin's own phasing-out deduction already in this project): if the employee's wages FOR THE PERIOD exceed this threshold, the exemption amount is $0 for that period entirely, not partially reduced. Booklet's own words: '$290,800... $0.00' in the annual row of the exemption table, with every other period's threshold being $290,800 divided by that period's count (verified: weekly 290,800/52=5,592.31 exact match, daily 290,800/260=1,118.46 exact match) -- confirmed after an initial extraction pass had the threshold VALUES shifted one row off from their period LABELS (the same class of column-shift artifact already documented elsewhere in this project), resolved by cross-checking against the document's own later prose statement ('if your annual wages exceed $290,800, your exemption amount will be phased out') as an independent anchor.

supplementalComment: Flat 5.99% (the top marginal rate) on supplemental wages paid separately from regular wages, per the booklet's own instruction ('The Supplemental withholding rate is 5.99%') — computed by flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() as an XX_SIT_SUPP line, with the bonus carved out of the regular base so it's taxed once. Scoped to a bonus paid on its OWN cheque; paid alongside regular wages, the ordinary tables run on the combined amount, which is what this state's own instruction calls for.
exemptComment: Rhode Island taxable income starts from federal AGI (R.I. Gen. Laws 44-30), which already nets out these categories at the federal level -- the same 'starts from a federal figure' inference tier as several other states in this project, not yet upgraded to a direct booklet quote naming each category.

reciprocity.rule: NONE. Rhode Island has no reciprocal withholding agreements with Massachusetts or Connecticut (its only bordering states) -- cross-source confirmed. The booklet does offer 'CONVENIENCE WITHHOLDING' (an employer may voluntarily withhold RI tax for an out-of-state RI resident employee as a courtesy), which is opt-in, not a reciprocity exemption.
reciprocity.convenienceWithholdingKnownGap: RESOLVED (2026-09-02): this is no longer RI-specific unmodelled behavior -- residenceStateWithholdingLine() in state.ts now computes it generically for every state via input.residenceStateWithholding.voluntary (or .nexus for the mandatory case), gated off whenever a real reciprocity exemption/swap already applies. See tests/engine.test.ts's 'Voluntary / nexus-based residence-state withholding' describe block. Trusts the caller's own assertion at face value -- no verification that the employer actually elected this, the same simplification this engine already makes for reciprocity certificates generally.

localIncomeTax.rule: NONE. No Rhode Island city or town levies a local income or wage tax.

stateDisabilityEmployee.$comment: TDI (Temporary Disability Insurance), which ALSO funds TCI (Temporary Caregiver Insurance, Rhode Island's paid-family-leave equivalent) -- the SAME single contribution funds both programs, structurally the same 'one tax, two benefit programs' shape already documented for California's SDI/PFL combination in this project. Reuses the existing generic stateDisabilityEmployeeTax() dispatch -- no new engine code needed. Rate DECREASED from 1.3% (2025) to 1.1% (2026); wage base INCREASED from $89,200 to $100,000 -- both real year-over-year changes, not typos, confirmed by two independent sources agreeing.

unemploymentInsurance.administeredBy: RI Department of Labor and Training (DLT)

verification: PROVEN via calculatePaycheck() against the booklet's own worked example ($87.57, weekly $2,195/single/1 exemption) plus additional hand-derived fixtures covering the exemption phase-out cliff and TDI. See tests/engine.test.ts, describe('Rhode Island').
knownGaps: STILL OPEN: whether this state's unemployment wage base excludes the same pretax categories as its income tax withholding (the engine currently applies exemptPretax to both) — elective deferrals are commonly included in the unemployment base while excluded from income tax.
Supplemental flat-5.99% method computed by flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() as an XX_SIT_SUPP line — see supplementalComment above.

Convenience withholding (opt-in RI withholding for out-of-state residents) documented but not modelled as a certificate mechanism. CLARIFIED (this pass): no new mechanism is needed. Convenience withholding is an agreement to withhold Rhode Island tax for someone working outside the state, and a caller obtains exactly that by resolving workState to RI for the payment — the engine then withholds RI tax on it in the ordinary way. What this engine deliberately does NOT do is decide on the employee's behalf that such an agreement exists, which is why there is no certificate flag: the agreement is the caller's fact, and setting the work state IS how it is expressed.

Supplemental wages, RESOLVED THIS PASS but with a caveat: RI's own booklet states both a flat 5.99% option (Section 12) and an aggregate-with-last-preceding-period option (Section 4), wired as the same dual-method employer choice Missouri already uses in this project. The 5.99% figure is ALSO exactly RI's own top bracket rate, so it is not certain this is a genuinely independent method rather than Section 12 restating what aggregation converges to for a high earner -- both paths are offered rather than picking one with more confidence than the source supports.

suiEmployer.$comment: Normalized employer-side unemployment parameters — the shape src/taxes/state.ts reads. The detailed unemploymentInsurance block above stays the record of research; this exists because that block's shape varies too much between states to compute from directly (wage bases as objects, industry-keyed rate maps, differently-named keys).
suiEmployer.wageBaseSource: 2026 taxable wage bases cross-checked against EY's published 2026 state-by-state table; where this file already carried a numeric wage base, the two agreed unless noted in wageBaseNote.
suiEmployer.newEmployerRateSource: This state's own unemploymentInsurance block above, researched in an earlier pass — kept in preference to any aggregate table.

supplementalWages.$comment: RI Section 12: "The Supplemental withholding rate is 5.99%." Modelled as UNCONDITIONAL (no employer election field) rather than optional, matching Ohio's own mandatory-flat-rate shape in this project: Section 12's own wording is declarative ("the rate IS 5.99%"), not permissive ("the employer MAY elect"), unlike Missouri's or California's own genuinely optional flat methods. See this file's own sources[] entry for the ambiguity against Section 4's aggregate-only description -- Section 4's aggregate option is not separately wired since this engine always resolves the flat rate first for a standalone supplemental payment once a supplementalWages config exists, so a supplementalAggregation block would be unreachable dead configuration here, not a real alternative path.
